newsitem.title: USA: Lott sees "difficulty" for China MFN votes.
newsitem.headline: Lott sees "difficulty" for China MFN votes.

text.p: Senate Majority Leader Trent Lott said allegations that China sought to influence the 1996 U.S. elections have complicated this year's vote on renewing China's Most Favored Nation trading status.
Lott told ABC-TV's "This Week" program the vote would likely face some difficulty in the House of Representatives and would be closer than generally expected in the Senate.
Lott urged the Clinton administration and the Democratic Party to stop stalling Congress in answering questions about the alleged influence-buying scheme of the Chinese government.

"If we don't have the end of the stonewalling by the Democrats on what happened with regard to foreign contributions and how was the Chinese government involved in trying to influence American elections, that could then fall over into the debate on China MFN," the Mississippi Republican said. "It's a very tough issue."

Republicans could not block a vote on China's Most Favored Nation status, Lott said, although he said lack of cooperation by the Clinton administration on a campaign finance probe by Sen. Fred Thompson's governmental affairs panel may jeopardize the vote.
The panel's Democrats on Thursday rejected a plan to grant immunity from prosecution to a group of Buddhist monks and nuns who may have made illegal contributions to the Democrats.
"It is in some difficulty, obviously, in the House," Lott said. "It may be closer in the Senate than anybody had anticipated."

Lott said he was inclined to support MFN, but would have to review developments related to China's takeover of Hong Kong in July and "also what we find out about an effort by foreign governments to influence American elections."

Lawmakers have expressed concerns about renewing Most Favored Nation status because of concerns about human rights abuses, nuclear technology transfers and the future of Hong Kong after the British colony comes under Chinese rule on July 1, as well as the $38 billion U.S. trade deficit with China last year.
Administration officials and Clinton have spoken in recent days of the dangers to both U.S. security and commercial interests if China's trade status is revoked.

The House Ways and Means Committee is expected to hold a hearing next week on China's trade status and vote on a resolution that would deny the trade privilege to Beijing. A committee aide said the panel is expected to send the measure to the full House for action later this month with a recommendation that their fellow lawmakers vote against it.

Last year the House upheld the president's decision to renew MFN by a comfortable 286-141 margin. The Senate never took up the issue. Speaker of the House Newt Gingrich has said he expects a closer vote this year.
Efforts in Congress to overturn the president on Most Favored Nation status have been unsuccessful since the 1989 Chinese army's bloody crackdown on pro-democracy demonstrators in Tiananmen Square.
